The Stanley Parable made me start reading books again.
No, I am not joking. let me elaborate.

There is a very daft achievement in this game that asks you to play it for the whole duration of a Tuesday. I wasn't going to tinker with my computers clock and BIOS settings JUST for an achievement (ahem), so I decided to do it the hard way.

Since this is a pretty big commitment and I didn't want to have to try it more than once, I made sure I would be ABSOLUTELY in-game for those 24 hours by:
* turning off all screensavers and sleep modes
" making sure Windows Update would not fuck me up (as best as I could)
* putting a weight on the "W" button of my keyboard to have the game constantly receive input
* not even alt-tabbing out of the game, just leave it and Steam as the only applications running

so that meant I could not use my PC for a whole day, which gave me the opportunity to reflect on things I always wanted to do but just never bothered to, such as reading books.

After finding my Kindle and bringing it back to life (had to perform CPR on the battery), I started reading The Three-Body Problem, a book I had bought years ago but always postponed reading. 

Oh, the joy of rediscovering the pleasure of reading a good book.
So now I have my PC back but I still read a couple of chapters everyday, so thank you The Stanley Parable for this opportunity.

Oh and the game is cool and all, very meta, breaks the 4th wall bla bla

tl;dr: The Stanley Parable held my computer hostage for 24 hours, so I started reading books again.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
[i]The Stanley Parable[/i] is a one of a kind game. You play as Stanley, an employee that has to press buttons. When suddenly, you stop and head out your office. A narrator describes your adventure and it's up to you to listen to him or not. Explore the office building and make different choices every playthrough and unlock all of the many endings possible!

[h1]The Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Beautiful[/b] - The graphics are decent, the lightning glorious, and walking through the building is pleasant to the eye.

[*][b]Choices[/b] - The best thing a game can do for you is let you be in control. The Stanley Parable makes you make your own story, every step of the way, and unlocking a different ending every time. Such decisions include taking the left or right door, going to the meeting or not, or turning off the evil machine... or not. Every action has a thing to say for the ending.

[*][b]Comical[/b] - The narrator says things that are sometimes very funny, the way he reacts when you disobey him and the scenes you encounter have some very rich monologue.

[*][b]Deep[/b] - It might not look like this the first time you play, but as you uncover different endings you will see the hidden meaning behind Stanley's story. The writing is very cleverly done, the existance of the narrator poses further questions, and the very nature of reality bends amongst different endings.
[/list]

[h1]The Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Repetitive up to a point[/b] - As the story forks at different intersections, you are bound to repeat parts of it until you reach the branching point. Some of the paths require waiting for long narrations to play, so you might become a little impatient along the process.

[*][b]Unconventional Achievements[/b] - Most achievements require a degree of witt to figure out what they want (or read a guide) but there are some that are really unnecessary, such as playing the game for the entire duration of a Tuesday, implying either BIOS Time Changing or leaving the PC idle for 24 hours, the [i]Unachiveable[/i], which requires configuration file tweaks and the [i]Go Outside[/i] which makes you not play for... 5 years. Of course, circumventable with a little sly techniques, but they are not achievements related to the game. They don't track progress or skill, they're just there to mess with you and waste your time.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
The Stanley Parable stand out amongst the rest of pshycological narratives and really puts the player in a position of power over his destiny, or at least gives him a very powerful delusion about it. Buy with confidence, it is an enjoyable experience.

[h1]Excellent production[/h1]

The Stanley Parable is a very unusual game. In the game we play the role of an office worker who wakes up and sees that the office he works in is empty. The narrator wants to help us in this difficult situation, who tries to lead us to the next rooms. And this is where the fun begins...

Because we don't have to listen to him, which gives us the freedom to play. Even though the game has no open world, we can get out of the way in many situations. Of course, we will still be accompanied by a narrator who tries to take us to where he wanted us to go before, but still it's up to us what we do.

Despite the lack of an open world, the game gives us a lot of opportunities, which allows us to have about 5 hours of fun. To show that 5 hours is a lot, it's a simple thread where we listen to the narrator can be completed in less than 5 minutes (there is even such an achievement). 5 hours with a great narrator is definitely not time wasted.

There's no need to talk about graphics here, in the game, because it's simple, but it doesn't matter much, because it's not the most important. The most important thing is the gameplay itself, listening to the narrator, who gets nervous when we do something not according to his thoughts, the desire to discover new rooms and look for new endings

[h1]Summary[/h1]

The Stanley Parable is a very good game. It is hilarious, interesting and addictive. Of course you can't say that it's a game that matches the biggest titles but you can still have fun with it and I think it's the perfect game for one evening.

On the other hand, Stanley was aware that the game was short, and once all the endings were reached he found himself uninterested in returning. Additionally, if Stanley wanted, he could find a multitude of Youtube videos that showed everything in the game for free.

In the end, Stanley decided to recommend the game. Stanley Parable is a unique, if not atypical game. You play as employee number 427; an employee who only pushes buttons as per the instructions of his superiors. Stanley, however, does not receive any orders one day, therefore, he gets up from his desk and starts investigating what exactly has happened.

And this is where you take control of him in this FPS which uses the well-known game engine called Source. Our protagonist immediately notices that nobody else is present in the office - he passes empty cubicles and corridors trying to find the answers.

There are no weapons in this game. No NPCs you can interact with. No objectives. No goals. Stanley Parable is about exploration. And this exploration, this journey of our white-collar worker is accompanied by the narrator's voice.

However, you will notice that the narrator tells Stanley, in advance, which door he is supposed to take. But you can refuse the command and go to the direction you desire. And this is the most crucial part of this game: it is about choices. Your choices.

And these choices can yield you at least a dozen endings. Endings that are funny, serious, sarcastic and some are even meant to be no more than mere easter eggs.

This is not something you'll spend dozens of hours with. No, Stanley Parable can be completed in a mere 30 minutes, still, it's worth the journey and the appreciation.

The Stanley Parable is a narrative story that stars, you guessed it, Stanley. Stanley works in a dead end job carrying out mindless tasks; and the story is told by one of the best narratives I have ever heard. Graphics isn't an important feature here, but that being said, it looks really nice. 
 
The design of the world is very well done, you are essentially in an office building, but it does a very clever thing where you can sometimes be walking around in a circle, and then all of a sudden the world changes, and you are somewhere else. This made the experience feel more real to me. You can make this game as easy or as difficult as you want. There is fifteen different stories and endings to the Stanley Parable, each of them is amazingly written, probably one of, if not the best story in gaming I've experienced and well worth playing.  It has taken me almost seven hours to play through all of the endings, and do all but one of the achievements. After you have played all of the endings though, there is probably no need to go replay any of the game again. 

Is the game worth £9, 99, sure? For about seven hours of gameplay and the amount of fun I had playing it; you cannot miss out on The Stanley Parable. This is now in my top ten favourite games of all time.

There really isn't anything that you can say about this except that it isn't a game.  Anyone buying it as such will be sorely disappointed.  What it IS is a brilliant commentary on not just gaming culture, but the thought processes of gamers themselves.

It really is brilliantly done, and superbly executed.  As a gamer, I felt a strange air of danger and menace throughout, as if something was going kick off and lead to some sort of battle for survival, and the game plays with this notion throughout, offering a number of different "endings".  The "good" ending (which I won't spoil) is a very well observed satire on game design and player choice.

It really is hard to write anything about the game without spoiling something!  All I can really say is - it's not for everyone.  Some people may look down on people who don't enjoy it or don't get it and that's not entirely fair.  The ideas and concept explored aren't hugely complex, but probably require a high level of self awareness and self criticism on the part of the player.

In summary - this is a sublime mix of art, gaming and genuine entertainment.

Any individual with even the slightest or most remote interest in video gaming as a medium of artistic expression must categorically play The Stanley Parable within their lifetime. It's, ostensibly, a re-release of the 2011 Half-Life 2 mod of the same name, and is still built on the Source engine and is, more or less, largely the same game but having been thoroughly redesigned in certain key ways, especially its themes and parts of its narrative structure.

The Stanley Parable (developed by a small indie studio named Galactic Cafe) is, essentially, as its demo states, "a game of endings". It's a game that poses some very important questions about the way games currently work - it's a parable (a story which illustrates a lesson), or rather a collection of parables each hidden within another. Each new playthrough represents a new part of the experience, revealing yet another of the game's many endings, each with a different existential or absurdist lesson that build into the game's broader thesis. 

It's also a game of choice, in that it proposes that ludic notions of "choice" and "free will" are inherently absurd in all games, since they don't actually represent any kind of meaningful or significant choice: they're just slightly different parts of the same overall plan that the game designer has laid out before you, and thus subordinate to his own intentions and choices; and therefore, inconsequential. You're still only just walking that path - in fact, all you ever do in the Stanley Parable is walk; literally. And when you do press the use button (which is for ludic purposes the mouse button, but in the original mod, was the 'E' button), you hear the unmistakable sound of a key being pressed. And as the intro and several endings exemplify, that is the nature of Stanley's job and ultimately, the nature of his existence and of our experience within the game: pressing buttons, both in-game and out of game.

It also has a lot to say about endings, and the way choices feed into those endings. By presenting us with a closed environment with very minimal and sparse mechanics, The Stanley Parable is able to present us with an environment so sparse and so limited that the "choices" we are offered seem that much more significant and that much more abundant; and the same goes for its endings. But as much as the choices themselves mean nothing, they also lead the player into the aforementioned endings. No ending has finality, and no ending presents a perfect victory for Stanley or the player. In fact, in almost all the endings the respective thematic conflict between Stanley and the Narrator remains entirely open, but no ending feeds into another in any capacity, underlining the lack of meaning the notion of multiple endings in games can offer. Games teach the player that anything but a perfect win-state is a failure, and that further playthroughs can objectively improve the conclusion of the story, be it through moral superiority or mechanical perfection. The Stanley Parable, in comparison, gives us subjective endings which can be interpreted freely which all invariably lead into a restart of the game. As the game itself states: "the end is never the end is never the end is never the end is never LOADING".

In the process, certain themes and concepts will be left underdeveloped; but isn't this the point of the game? Asking questions that only subsequent explorations of the game by way of critical commentary or subsequent works in the same vein (perhaps by Galactic Cafe, or other designers) will be able to answer? Leaving its own ideas open to interpretation and exploration? I certainly think so. And so, it's definitely worth experiencing for yourself. Set your prejudices regarding "walking simulators" or "ungames" aside and walk into The Stanley Parable without any expectations but those the game designer creates for himself and for his own vision.

[h1]Originally conceived as a Half-Life mod in 2011 and released as it's own game in 2013, [i]The Stanley Parable[/i] is not only a member of Half-Life's legacy but also an interesting insight into gameplay, creating an approximated meta-dialogue between developer and gamer as very few titles manage to do[/h1]

[list]
[h1]Pros[/h1]
[*]Ascerbic and witty dialogue
[*]Superlative voice acting
[*]Story that offers multiple branches of narrative

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[*]Reincarnation becomes repetitive
[/list]

[i]“The logical flaws and inconsistencies that riddled the tale, far from making him doubt its veracity finally convinced him that it might indeed be true; for life is like that.” 
― Tom Holt, Expecting Someone Taller[/i]

The Stanley Parable, isn’t so much a game as it is an exploration of what games are and how they function. It’s constant self-awareness and subtle humour create an experience that isn’t quite like any other, constantly challenging your perceptions of your choices and movement, just as much as it exposes the artificiality of such freedom. Setting all of this within a self-determined narrative that explores multiple endings and their effects on your character, and his ultimate quest for meaning.

[i]“He made a conscious decision not to think about it, and accordingly spent the rest of his shift thinking about nothing else.” 
― Tom Holt, Doughnut[/i]

The Stanley Parable, explores the life of one Stanley, quick to portray his middle-class, bourgeoisie position, happy to follow orders and work within the confines and comfort of familiarity. It is only when this normality is disrupted that Stanley is prompted to leave his comfortable confines, and search for something more. The game critiques Stanley throughout his adventure, and through him the player. Choose to be contrarian and the omniscient  British narrator will intervene to make your position more difficult. Following his instructions however will result in him being more amenable, and assisting you. It’s amusing to note that following orders leads to a more satisfactory conclusion than disobeying. It’s a small conceit to those who pay attention to the grander themes, and plays to the games irony and satiricial humour.

[i]“That's the problem with running away, said the little voice. No matter where you go, you have to take yourself with you; and if yourself is constitutionally incapable of leaving well enough alone and not worrying if the rest of the world is weirder than ferret ragout, where the hell is the point?” 
― Tom Holt[/i]
As a walking simulator the mechanics are limited to exploration through simple movement and observation. The mouse controls the camera and your ability to perceive your environment, and the basic control structures to turn left and right and walk. Its game mechanics at their utmost basic level, with some small witticisms regarding certain movements such as jump being disabled. And true to the nature of this genre, not much more is really required to experience the story on offer. It’s interactivity stripped to its naked basics and in so doing it challenges the boundaries of interactivity and games purely by the fact that it removes more complex options and provides you only what you [i]need[/i] to make choices.

Wandering the hallways will result in varied responses from your vociferous guide. His narration an amusing counterpoint to your exploration. His initial omniscience largely implied by his stentorian and authoritative tone, is quickly shown to be as much of an illusion as the supposed narrative of the game itself. Challenging him, or working with him, forms as much a part of gameplay as it does with other such narrators including GLaDOS and SHODAN. These guiding principles assist one with finding the multiple endings the game has on offer as well as their various permutations. The karmic cycle of resetting and re-exploring leads to these variations and previous choices can lead to more exclusive endings. Shaping Stanley as either an agent of freewill and compatriot to his narrator or as a subservient drone to a totalitarian dictator, creates multiple possibilities to ‘play’ with.

The Stanley Parable is something unique, and a formula largely unreplicated by other developer studios. It is also not completely to the taste of all, with its satiricial wit and dry gameplay. It could very easily go over the head of many gamers, particularly in a modern climate where games are argued to be only a means of escapism and cannot be viewed critically. The socio-political and existential merits of such a title as [i]The Stanley Parable[/i] would be sorely missed. If however such things are of interest then [i]The Stanley Parable[/i] is well worth a playthrough as are other games by the studio such as the free title [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/409160/Dr_Langeskov_The_Tiger_and_The_Terribly_Cursed_Emerald_A_Whirlwind_Heist/] Dr. Langeskov, The Tiger, and The Terribly Cursed Emerald: A Whirlwind Heist[/url].

The Stanley Parable is a ground-up remake of the cult Half-Life 2 mod and expands it in a dozen directions without altering its fundamentals. It is one of those "first-person walking" games in which you wander around a completely non-violent experience exploring the environment and unravelling the story, like Dear Esther.
You are Stanley, an office worker. Stanley has the job to push buttons on command until some day those commands abruptly stop. Stanley is leaving his desk to investigate, his actions are directed by a narrator who guides him through the office facility to discover the truth.
The Stanley Parable is a game about walking from A to B. As you approach a pair of doors, the narrator will indicate that Stanley takes the left one. Whether you do and how you decide to follow up your revolt or acquiescence, tilts the game towards wildly different conclusions. A playthrough may only take minutes, but The Stanley Parable has a lot of choices and a lot of different endings. It will take a few hours to see everything and every ending.
At each of the game's many intersections, you can follow the narrator's instruction or ignore it and face the consequences of your petty resistance. Each combination of choices leads to something unique. Some of these "endings" are lighthearted, some are absurd and many centre around the narrator's attempts to get back to his story.
The Stanley Parable has not the best Source Engine graphics. Many of the environments are bland, but deliberately so. Delightful hidden details show their faces everywhere if you are willing to look.
The best part of The Stanley Parable is the voice acting of the omnipotent Narrator. He plays witness to every move which do you make. From a kindly, yet firm, guiding hand at the start of the game to an acerbic wit if you ignore him, the Narrator really adds a soul to the world of The Stanley Parable.
I enjoyed the game and I would recommend the game to people who want to try out something different instead of the normal games, but I would advice everyone to try out The Stanley Parable Demo before buying the game. It will tell you nothing about the main game, but you should then be able to decide if the game is something for you or not.
If you should still be unsure, you can also try the free mod, to make your final decision. The mod does not actually require Half-Life 2 on PC, only the Source SDK.

This is the story of a man named Stanley,

Stanley worked for a company in a big building where he was Employee #427.

Employee #427's job was simple: he sat at his desk in Room 427 and he pushed buttons on a keyboard.

Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order.

This is what Employee #427 did every day of every month of every year, and although others may have considered it soul rending,

Stanley relished every moment that the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job.

And Stanley was happy.

And then one day, something very peculiar happened.

Something that would forever change Stanley;

Something he would never quite forget.

He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he had realized not one single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow.

No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say 'hi'. Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation.

Something was very clearly wrong. Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time.

But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.

This short review/analysis contains spoilers about the game. Stop reading if you want to have a fresh experience with the game. Everything below is my speculation, don't take them as definitive facts.
The Stanley Parable is everything and beyond video games. It's a giant commentary on todays game development philosophy. Throughout its unexpected span and twisty narrative, it has a clear message - there are problems with narrative in video games, which we have not addressed yet.
In recent years we have seen a great amount of open world/sand box games. But there hasn't been shortage in linear games with strict control over players actions. Invisible walls or direct threatening by the game if you go off the map, even in scenarios where the level design suggests more freedom than the available and, but not limited to - bugging out the whole game or level by reaching unexpected locations are common practices in multiplayer and even in singleplayer games since decades.
The layout of the office (which is briefly explained in the museum, behind the scenes room) is designed and created with the mind that the dialogue and attention span of the player would balance and lead to the first sense of conflict - the two doors.
This first dilemma is presented geniously - with a confident and calm voice. At this point the narrator is still following the hardcoded written script. Which is what I describe as the main and simple story the whole Stanely Parable is based around - there is a problem, the protagonist decides to end the tyranny of the evil force and it concludes with a happy ending.
The simple story has cartoonish elements. Toward the end of it, it cultivates exaggerated tone and willingly becomes boring, it's purpose is to show the most basic and at the same time intriguing story. But only if the player obeys/follows the steps the given by the narrator. 
Not obeying the narrative, leads to all sorts of interesting results, which ultimately don't explain the whole picture of The Stanley Parable, which is left to players imagination. The game doesn't feel the need to address any of the questions which the audience asks frantically after playing it. The same happened in the demonstration, particularly in the 'Escape elevator' sequence.
Throughout the exploration/ending hunting there are many sections where the nature of narration and design in games is examined and often made fun out of.
Many actions, which are not part of the hardcoded script, of the player are directly commentated by the narrator.
Like the 'Broom closet' - this room has no place in the whole game. In traditional game narrative it would be a waste of time - there isn't a collectable or extra life and if the player decides to explore it, the game would punish him for doing so. But here, the comedic nature of TSP rewards the player for paying attention to it, even if it is only a piece of dialogue.
Achievements are another device with which the The Stanley Parable mocks the current video game industry. Take the 'Click on door 430 five times' for example  - a great way to address the ridiculous amount of pointless achievements in some games. Or 'Unachievable' - an obvious phantom which doesn't have a solution. It is created solely that particular part of the player audience grinds through the game, desperately trying to get it.
So, how does The Stanley Parable get away with being so rude to every aspect in the modern video game industry, while being part of it?
Its complete and constant self awareness makes TSP simply perfect. It is written and executed exceptionally well. It deflects most of the criticism, directed at it, simply by being one.

The Stanley Parable is a wholly unique game. I almost hesitate to call it a game, since it's only interactive by the strictest legal definition, and you merely move around while listening to a narrator talk, deciding whether to do what it says or not. It can play out in some truly interesting ways, but if you follow the "true" ending, the entire game will be over in a matter of 10 minutes. There's even an achievement for beating it in under 4:22 (which you can't do for the first few playthroughs anyway, so don't worry about it yet).

The story is fairly interesting, and there are a lot of different "endings" you can get, but the base of it is repeating the same office section over and over and trying out different choices to see what happens.

It's thoroughly experimental, and while I do tend to enjoy games that give players choices like that, this one was just way too short, and didn't really do much with its central theme. I'm not joking when I say that you could follow the narrator's instructions, finish the game in 10 minutes, and be left thinking "wait, was that really it!?" 

The true fun in the game, though, is in messing with the narrator. He tells you to do Thing A, so you do Thing B. He tells you to do something, so you do nothing. He gets irritated, bored, upset, etc. The narrator is undeniably the star of the show in this game, and it certainly can be fun to mess with him. There's unique dialog for every branch you take, which is impressive. That being said, it felt like some of his speeches went on just a little too long, but I had fun anyway.

This is one that you really have to try for yourself to see if you'll like it. I don't think it's as overwhelmingly awesome as the general consensus seems to be, but I enjoyed it for what it was: An experimental little deviation from the norm. There's a demo to try out, so maybe do that?

Oh, also, if you want the achievements, be aware that you have to fire it up (you NEED to start it at least once), then not play it again for 5 years. I'm serious. There were threads in the community hub around the game's 5 year anniversary talking about how excited they were to finally be able to play it. Madness.

Stanley, stanley, stanley. Stanley... stanley, stanley. Stanley. Stanley, stanley... stanley. Stanley!!!

That is all. Now can I go home?
